title: Brick Breaker
description: In this project, you'll build the classic arcade game Brick Breaker from scratch! You will learn how to control sprites with the mouse, use cloning to create lots of objects, and keep track of a score.

steps.title: See it in Action!
steps.content:
Before we start building, let's see what the final game looks like! Brick Breaker (also known as Breakout) is a classic arcade game where you control a paddle to bounce a ball and destroy all the bricks.

Watch the short video below to understand the main goal. Notice how the paddle moves, how the ball bounces, and what happens when it hits a brick.
hints: There's no code for this step! Just watch the video and get excited to build your own version.
Think like a game developer: we'll need to create a player paddle, a moving ball, and lots of breakable bricks. Let's build them one by one!

steps.title: Create the Paddle
steps.content:
Every game needs a hero! Our hero is the paddle. Let's start by creating a new sprite that will act as our paddle.

First, delete the default Cat sprite. We don't need a cat in space! Then, choose a new sprite from the Scratch library. The 'Button 3' sprite is a great choice for a paddle, but feel free to pick any you like! Rename this sprite to 'Paddle' so our code is easy to read later.
hints: To delete a sprite, click on the small trash can icon on the sprite in the sprite list below the stage.
To create a new sprite, click the 'Choose a Sprite' button (the cat head icon) in the bottom right.
To rename a sprite, click on the 'Sprite' name box above the scripting area and type in 'Paddle'.

steps.title: Position the Paddle
steps.content:
Our paddle shouldn't be flying all over the screen. It needs to stay locked at the bottom. We'll write our first script to lock its vertical position.

In game design, coordinates are like a giant piece of graph paper. Y controls Up and Down, while X controls Left and Right.

Grab a `when green flag clicked` block. Then, use `set y to ()` and type in `-150`. Why just Y? Because we want to lock it at the bottom so it can't fly away, but we want to leave X (left-and-right) free for the player to control!
hints: The `when green flag clicked` block is the universal 'Start Game' button in Scratch. Find it in the yellow Events category.
The `set y to ()` block is in the blue Motion category.
A Y-position of `0` is the exact middle of the screen. Using a negative number like `-150` pushes it down to the bottom.
finishedCode:
when green flag clicked
set y to (-150)

steps.title: Follow the Mouse
steps.content:
Now for the fun part! We need the paddle to follow our mouse pointer so we can control it.

To do this, grab a `forever` loop. Inside the loop, add a `set x to ()` block. Then, go to Sensing and drop `mouse x` inside the hole.

Why do we need a forever loop? Computers are super fast, but they only do exactly what you say. If we didn't use a loop, the computer would set the paddle to your mouse position exactly one time when the game starts, and then never update it again! The `forever` loop acts like a guard on duty, constantly checking the mouse position every single frame.
hints: A `forever` loop is found in the orange Control category.
The `set x to ()` block controls the left-and-right position.
The `mouse x` block is a special sensor that always knows where your mouse pointer is.
finishedCode:
when green flag clicked
set y to (-150)
forever
  set x to (mouse x)
end

steps.title: Add the Ball
steps.content:
Let's add our ball! Choose a new sprite from the library (the 'Ball' sprite is perfect) and rename it 'Ball'.

We want the ball to start directly in the middle of the screen every time we play. Using another `when green flag clicked` event, tell the ball to `go to x: (0) y: (0)`.

Then, to make sure it doesn't just fall straight down, we need to give it a starting angle. Use the `point in direction (45)` block so it fires off diagonally!
hints: The `go to x: () y: ()` block acts like a teleporter. `x:0 y:0` is the exact 'bullseye' center of the stage.
The `point in direction ()` block sets the angle the sprite is facing. You'll find it in Motion.
finishedCode:
when green flag clicked
go to x: (0) y: (0)
point in direction (45)

steps.title: Make the Ball Move
steps.content:
A ball isn't very useful if it's just sitting there. Let's make it move!

In the Ball's script, add a `forever` loop. Inside the loop, add a `move (10) steps` block. In Scratch, "steps" really means "pixels per frame."

To stop the ball from flying off the screen and getting lost forever, add the special `if on edge, bounce` block inside the loop. Why use this block? Because otherwise, we would have to write complex math to figure out when it hits a wall and calculate the reflection angles ourselves. This block is a superpower that does all that math for us!
hints: The `move () steps` block makes the sprite move forward in whatever direction it is currently facing.
Make sure both `move` and `if on edge, bounce` are securely inside the `forever` loop, or the ball will only move 10 pixels and stop!
finishedCode:
when green flag clicked
go to x: (0) y: (0)
point in direction (45)
forever
  move (10) steps
  if on edge, bounce
end

steps.title: Bounce off the Paddle
steps.content:
Now we need the ball to recognize when it hits the paddle and bounce off it.

Inside the Ball's `forever` loop, add an `if <> then` block. For the condition, use the `touching ?` block.

When it touches the paddle, we want it to bounce upwards. Use `point in direction (pick random (-60) to (60))` to force the ball to face the top of the screen at a random angle.

Crucial Step: Add a `move (15) steps` block right underneath it. Why? If you don't push the ball away instantly, it might get 'stuck' inside the paddle, vibrating and glitching out because the code triggers over and over incredibly fast!
hints: The `if <> then` block is how a computer makes decisions. Find it in the orange Control category.
The green `pick random () to ()` block is in Operators. In Scratch, straight up is 0 degrees. -60 to 60 gives us a nice upward fan shape!
finishedCode:
when green flag clicked
go to x: (0) y: (0)
point in direction (45)
forever
  move (10) steps
  if on edge, bounce
  if <touching [Paddle v]?> then
    point in direction (pick random (-60) to (60))
    move (15) steps
  end
end

steps.title: Create the Bricks
steps.content:
Time for the main event: the bricks!

Why use Clones? Imagine if you made 50 separate brick sprites. If you wanted to change their color, you'd have to edit 50 different scripts! Clones let us write the code once for a 'master brick' that acts like a factory blueprint, stamping out copies of itself.

Create a new 'Brick' sprite. Start with `when green flag clicked` and `hide` the master brick. Then, set a starting position for your grid. We'll use two `repeat` loops (a loop inside a loop!). The inside loop stamps out a row of 10 bricks, moving right each time. The outside loop drops down to the next row and repeats it 5 times!
hints: In your loops, use `create clone of myself` to make a copy. After making a clone, `change x by (48)` to move to the next position in the row.
After the inner row is finished, `set x` back to the starting left side and `change y by (-24)` to move down to the next row.
Clones need their own starting instructions! Grab the `when I start as a clone` hat block from the Control section. Under it, simply put a `show` block to make the clone visible.
finishedCode:
// This script acts as the Factory Blueprint
when green flag clicked
hide
go to x: (-210) y: (140)
repeat (5)
  repeat (10)
    create clone of[myself v]
    change x by (48)
  end
  set x to (-210)
  change y by (-24)
end

steps.title: Break the Bricks
steps.content:
Let's make those bricks breakable!

This code goes in the 'Brick' sprite, under the `when I start as a clone` block. Add a `forever` loop, and check `if `. If a brick clone gets hit by the ball, we want to destroy it using the `delete this clone` block. This completely erases that copy from the computer's memory.

Important: Don't forget to go back to the Ball's code! Add an `if touching Brick` block in the Ball's forever loop, and make it bounce downward by using `point in direction (pick random (120) to (240))`.
hints: Make sure this new logic is under the `when I start as a clone` block. Each individual clone needs to constantly run its own hit-detection check.
When a clone is deleted, it's gone for good! The `delete this clone` block is found at the very bottom of the Control category.
To make the ball bounce in the Ball's script, use angles that point down. In Scratch, 180 is straight down, so 120 to 240 works perfectly!
finishedCode:
when I start as a clone
show
forever
  if <touching [Ball v]?> then
    delete this clone
  end
end

steps.title: Add a Score
steps.content:
What's a game without a score? Let's track how many bricks the player has broken. For this, we need a Variable.

Think of a variable as a digital sticky note that the computer uses to remember a number. Go to the Variables category and click 'Make a Variable'. Name it `Score` and make sure it's 'For all sprites'.

When the game starts, you must `set [Score] to (0)`. Why? Because computers have great memories! If you end a game with 50 points, the computer will remember that 50 the next time you play unless you tell it to reset.

Finally, in the 'Brick' sprite, right before a clone deletes itself, tell it to `change [Score] by (1)`.
hints: A good place for the `set [Score] to (0)` block is in the Stage's script area (or the Paddle's start script) under a `when green flag clicked` event.
In the Brick's script, when the ball touches it, you `change [Score] by (1)` and then `delete this clone`. If you delete the clone first, the code stops running and the score won't change!
finishedCode:
// In the Brick sprite
when I start as a clone
show
forever
  if <touching [Ball v]?> then
    change [Score v] by (1)
    delete this clone
  end
end

steps.title: Extension: Multi-Hit Bricks
steps.content:
You have a working game, but let's make it better! Let's make some bricks stronger so they take multiple hits to break. We will use Costumes as a form of 'health'.

Go into your Brick's Costumes tab. Duplicate your brick costume, and draw some cracks on it using the paintbrush tool! Name your two costumes `Healthy` and `Cracked`.

When a clone starts, `switch costume to (Healthy)`. Now change your collision code: Instead of immediately deleting, check `if `. If it is, `switch costume to (Cracked)`. Otherwise, `delete this clone`!
hints: You can find the `switch costume to ()` block in the Looks category.
To check the costume name, use an `if <> then else` block from the Control category. Put an `=` operator inside the hexagon.
Your condition will be `if < (costume name) = (Healthy) > then` switch to Cracked, `else` delete clone!
finishedCode:
// In the Brick sprite
when I start as a clone
switch costume to (Healthy v)
show
forever
  if <touching [Ball v]?> then
    if <(costume [name v]) =[Healthy]> then
      switch costume to (Cracked v)
    else
      change [Score v] by (1)
      delete this clone
    end
    // Add a tiny wait so the ball doesn't instantly double-hit!
    wait (0.1) seconds
  end
end

steps.title: Extension: The Apple Power-up
steps.content:
Let's add power-ups! We want random Apples to drop from destroyed bricks. If the paddle catches an apple, the paddle gets wider.

First, create an 'Apple' sprite. Make it hidden at the start. Go back to your Brick sprite. When a brick deletes itself, add `if <(pick random (1) to (5)) = (1)> then create clone of [Apple]`. Why? This gives the brick a 1-in-5 chance to drop an apple!

In the Apple sprite, tell the clones to go to the destroyed brick's position, show themselves, and forever `change y by (-5)` to fall. If it touches the paddle, use `broadcast (Powerup)` and delete the apple!
hints: The `broadcast ()` block acts like a walkie-talkie, sending a hidden signal to all other sprites in the game.
In your Paddle sprite, use the `when I receive [Powerup]` hat block. Make it `change size by (20)` so it gets wider!
To make the apple drop exactly where the brick was, use `set x to (x position)` and `set y to (y position)` before you `create clone of [Apple]` in the brick script.

steps.title: Extension: A Lives System
steps.content:
Currently, if the ball hits the bottom edge, it just bounces forever. Let's make the game challenging by giving the player exactly 3 lives.

Create a `Lives` variable. `Set [Lives] to (3)` when the flag is clicked. Next, draw a thin red box at the very bottom of the screen to act as the 'Lava' zone.

In your Ball's script, check `if `. If it is, `change [Lives] by (-1)`. Then force the ball to `go to x: (0) y: (0)` and `wait (1) seconds` to give the player a breather before it starts moving again. If Lives ever equals 0, `stop [all]` to trigger Game Over!
hints: You can create a new sprite and draw a long red rectangle for your Lava zone. Place it horizontally at `y: -175` so it sits just below the paddle.
Make sure your `if <touching (Lava) ?>` check is inside the Ball's `forever` loop alongside its movement blocks.

steps.title: You Win!
steps.content:
Congratulations! You've built a full Brick Breaker game packed with awesome features. You've learned about mouse controls, cloning, variables, collision detection, and broadcasting.

Show your game to your friends and teacher, and let them test out your Power-ups and Lives system!
hints: To check for a win, you could have a script in the Stage that checks `forever if <(Score) = (total number of bricks)>`. Then play a victory sound!
